name: Picture Superiority Effect
description: Pictures are typically remembered better than equivalent verbal material. Visual representations can leave a stronger memory trace than text alone, especially when they provide an additional code or cue for retrieval.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to tutorials, onboarding, diagrams, icon-plus-label systems, illustrated instructions, and content meant to be remembered later; it supports using visuals as memory aids, not replacing all text with icons.
prevalence_note: Widely reflected in presentation, content, learning, and onboarding guidance even when the formal term is omitted; it is more common in practice than many other memory-effect labels.

findings.description: In free-recall memory experiments, pictures were remembered better than verbal materials, directly backing the picture-superiority effect while leaving open whether imagery or dual coding best explains the mechanism.
findings.source_title: Picture superiority in free recall: Imagery or dual coding?

applications.title: Adobe Podcast AI's abstract illustration undermining recall
applications.description: Adobe Podcast AI's marketing uses an illustration described as too abstract to comprehend, presented as a case where a stylized visual works against the picture-superiority effect rather than for it -- a missed opportunity relative to a concrete, literal product image.
applications.ethical_note: A pure visual-communication effectiveness issue with no persuasion angle -- an overly abstract illustration is a clarity problem, not a deceptive or manipulative one, included here specifically as the negative counterpart to the ChatGPT entry in this same wave.

applications.title: ChatGPT using realistic product screenshots instead of abstract illustration
applications.description: ChatGPT's marketing features literal screenshots of the product running on mobile and desktop, rather than an abstract graphic -- a concrete, realistic image intended to be easier to recall and understand than a stylized illustration would be.
applications.ethical_note: An honest, literal representation of the actual product -- showing users exactly what they'll get rather than an idealized or abstract stand-in, which also happens to align with what the effect says is more memorable.

applications.title: Google's near-identical icons for Meet, Chat, Drive, and Calendar diluting recognition
applications.description: Google uses visually similar icon styles across distinct products (Meet, Chat, Drive, Calendar), which the source frames as reducing the picture-superiority effect's benefit -- when images look too alike, the distinctiveness that makes a picture more memorable than text is undermined.
applications.ethical_note: A visual-differentiation issue with no persuasion angle -- icons that look too similar make it harder to tell products apart at a glance, a usability cost rather than an ethical one.
